newsitem.title: CHINA: World parliamentarians' meeting opens in China.
newsitem.headline: World parliamentarians' meeting opens in China.

text.p: BEIJING, Sept 16 (Reuter ) - An international meeting of parliamentarians opened in China on Monday with calls for greater protection of human rights worldwide and action to ensure food for all.

Delegates to the 96th conference of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) would make a crucial contribution to the momentum for international change, said IPU president Ahmed Fathy Sorour in an opening speech.

"The right to food is the right to life itself... Without securing the right to life no other human right will hold any significance," Sorour told delegates and officials in Beijing's cavernous Great Hall of the People.
"I am confident that your deliberations will focus on a detailed plan of action containing feasible and concrete proposals that all states should be committed to carry out," he said.

Delegates to the conference, a talking shop that will allow formal and informal discussions among around 600 members of parliament from around the world, should try to find ways to guarantee food in an age of increasing globalisation, he said.
The five-day meeting will be the first time China has permitted open debate on human rights by foreigners since the U.N. World Conference on Women in Beijing last year.
China rejects most foreign criticism of its human rights record as interference in its internal affairs and routinely refuses visas to rights groups it considers hostile.

Apart from human rights and food issues, the conference will also choose a supplementary item for discussion from proposals ranging from a ban on anti-personnel mines to U.S. laws aimed at cutting foreign investment in Cuba, Iran and Libya.

An emergency proposal from Baghdad for the parliamentarians to debate recent U.S. attacks on Iraq will also be considered but would need approval from 80 percent of the members before it can be formally tabled for debate.
United Nations ambassador Joseph Reed appealed for support from parliamentarians in the U.N. battle for funding and political support.
Reed pointedly thanked China for paying its U.N. dues on time and mourned the United States' reluctance to do likewise.

"The United Nations is still facing the worst and most protracted financial crisis in its history. As of 31 August, arrears in payment for the regular and peace-keeping budgets amounted to almost $3.0 billion," he said at the opening ceremony.
"I appeal to you, parliamentarians of the world, to continue to give us the support we need," he said.
